name: DIM (diindolylmethane)

card.summary: A broccoli-derived compound sold as an estrogen-metabolism supplement; the appearance and hormone claims are mostly untested in humans.
card.note: Registered human trials concern cancer and other conditions, not appearance or physique.

quick.overview:
DIM is a compound the body forms when it digests indole-3-carbinol, which is found in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and cabbage. It is sold as a dietary supplement, and in bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles it is promoted as a way to influence how estrogen is metabolised.
Laboratory research has examined its possible biological effects, mostly in cancer models. No published trial has tested DIM for appearance, muscle or body-composition outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say DIM shifts estrogen breakdown toward metabolites they regard as favourable. In laboratory work it has been reported to inhibit histone deacetylase enzymes and to bind weakly to cannabinoid receptors [1]. Whether these effects occur at supplement intakes in people, or change appearance, has not been established.
quick.risks: DIM is sold as a dietary supplement in the US rather than as an approved drug. Safety data in healthy users are limited to small early-phase trial registrations. A homeopathic menopause product listing DIM as one ingredient carries a label advising people who are pregnant or breast-feeding to ask a health professional first [2].

lead: 3,3'-Diindolylmethane (DIM) is a compound formed in the body from indole-3-carbinol, which arises when cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage and kale are chopped or chewed. Stomach acid converts the indole-3-carbinol into DIM and related products [1][15]. It is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement.

In bodybuilding and hormone-focused communities, DIM is marketed and discussed as a way to steer estrogen metabolism toward what proponents call the favourable "2-hydroxy" pathway, in the hope of a leaner, less puffy look, with fewer estrogen-related effects such as water retention. Laboratory research has examined its biological effects, particularly in cancer models, and Wikipedia notes that it has been studied as a histone deacetylase inhibitor in vitro [1].

Human research on DIM and estrogen metabolites includes a 2023 randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 60 premenopausal women that also measured body fat, and two large retrospective laboratory-database studies that compared urinary estrogen profiles of DIM users and non-users [12][13][14]. Registered clinical trials list small early-phase studies in cancer, lupus, thyroid disease and healthy volunteers [3][4][5][6].

Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center describes DIM as the most studied metabolite of indole-3-carbinol, lists cancer prevention, estrogen metabolism and detoxification as its claimed purposes, and states that clinical data are limited [11].
infobox: Formed from indole-3-carbinol in cruciferous vegetables [1]
Sold as a dietary supplement in the US
Oral supplement, alone or in combination or specially formulated products [15]
Urinary 2-OH:16-OH estrogen ratio rose in some studies [13][15]

paras: People who take DIM do so mainly in the hope of influencing how the body handles estrogen, which in the communities that discuss it is linked to leaner-looking physiques, less puffiness and a more androgen-dominant look in men. These are the claims made by marketers and users of the supplement; the Wikipedia article on DIM describes laboratory research on its possible biological effects, particularly anti-cancer mechanisms, rather than body composition or appearance.[1]

DIM has the chemical formula C17H14N2 and a molar mass of about 246 g/mol [1]. It is not eaten directly in meaningful amounts; it arises when stomach acid converts indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables [1]. Supplements deliver DIM itself, in some products in specially formulated forms.

Wikipedia notes that DIM and its precursor indole-3-carbinol are under laboratory research for possible biological effects, and lists standard chemical hazard labelling for the pure compound (a GHS warning for skin and eye irritation and respiratory irritation); these refer to handling the chemical, not to supplement use.[1]

In vitro work reported that DIM acts as an inhibitor of histone deacetylases 1, 2 and 3, and that it binds weakly to the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2 [1]. A 2023 laboratory study reported that DIM reduced biofilms of Streptococcus mutans, a bacterium involved in dental plaque; as of 2025, Wikipedia notes that no clinical trial had confirmed an effect on plaque in people [1].

The estrogen angle is the one that matters for people who take DIM for physique reasons. Memorial Sloan Kettering reports that DIM changed estrogen urinary metabolite profiles in some premenopausal and postmenopausal women, including women with a history of early-stage breast cancer [11]. In one trial of tamoxifen-treated patients, DIM raised a favourable estrogen metabolite ratio but also lowered levels of tamoxifen metabolites; the center states that the effect of DIM on breast cancer risk is unknown [11]. These findings concern metabolite ratios in clinical populations, not body composition or appearance, and the same source notes that DIM may alter the results of estrogen urinary metabolite tests [11].

The Linus Pauling Institute explains the hypothesis: 16-alpha-hydroxyestrone is described as highly estrogenic and 2-hydroxyestrone as weakly estrogenic, so shifting metabolism toward the latter has been proposed to lower the risk of estrogen-sensitive cancers [15]. Controlled trials of indole-3-carbinol consistently raised the urinary 2-hydroxyestrone ratio, whereas case-control and cohort studies found no significant link between these ratios and breast or endometrial cancer risk [15]. Other proposed anti-estrogenic mechanisms include aryl hydrocarbon receptor-mediated degradation of estrogen receptor alpha and reduced aromatase expression in some breast cell lines [15].

sections.h: Human studies of estrogen profile and body fat
paras: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT02525159) in 60 premenopausal Mexican women with a low urinary estrogen metabolite ratio supplemented DIM for 30 days, with urine collected at baseline, day 30 and 30 days after stopping [12]. The DIM group did not significantly raise the ratio at day 30, with a non-significant upward trend 30 days after stopping, but showed a greater fall in body fat percentage than placebo (p = 0.04) [12]. The authors concluded DIM was ineffective at raising the ratio at the dose tested and called for further studies on dose, timeframe and effects on body fat [12].

A 2024 retrospective cohort study compared 909 premenopausal DIM users with 18,385 non-users using dried-urine hormone testing, and found nearly every estrogen and metabolite differed between groups; in 53 women with results before and after starting DIM, estrone, estradiol, estriol and 16-hydroxyestrone changed and the 2-hydroxy to 16-hydroxy ratio rose [13]. A 2025 retrospective study of 1,458 postmenopausal women using a transdermal estradiol patch, 108 of whom also took DIM, found DIM users differed on 6 of 10 urinary metabolites and recommended that providers ask patients about DIM use [14]. These studies are observational and report urinary profiles, not appearance outcomes [13][14].

In small studies of cervical precancer, one pilot found no clinical improvement with DIM and a larger trial of 551 women found DIM did not promote HPV clearance or prevent progression, according to the Linus Pauling Institute [15]. The same source reports that DIM appeared in blood about two hours after a dose and cleared within 24 hours, and that formulations to improve absorption are being developed [15].

Memorial Sloan Kettering lists case reports of visual impairment (central serous chorioretinopathy) in a healthy woman after two months of high daily intake, which resolved about eight weeks after stopping, a rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, an ischemic stroke in a 38-year-old woman and pulmonary embolism with deep vein thrombosis in a 65-year-old man, each associated with DIM use [11]. It reports that one study showed a significant decrease in serum endoxifen, an active tamoxifen metabolite, and that DIM may reduce the effectiveness of drugs handled by CYP450 enzymes or the MDR1 transporter [11]. The center advises that women who are pregnant, planning pregnancy or nursing should not take DIM because of possible hormonal effects, and that women on birth control pills consult a healthcare professional first [11].

The Linus Pauling Institute reports mild adverse effects in studies of indole-3-carbinol and DIM, including gastrointestinal symptoms in 5 of 20 women after single higher doses, a skin rash and slight liver enzyme rises in small numbers of women, and notes that safety in pregnancy and lactation has not been established; it also reports preliminary evidence of possible CYP1A2 induction and that acid-suppressing drugs may reduce formation of DIM [15]. In animal studies, indole-3-carbinol enhanced carcinogen-induced tumors when given after the carcinogen and inhibited them when given before or with it, and some experts have urged caution about widespread supplement use [15].

A 2023 randomized placebo-controlled trial of 60 premenopausal women reported a greater fall in body fat percentage with DIM than placebo over 30 days, without a significant change in the urinary estrogen metabolite ratio [12]. No studies found that test DIM for muscle, hormone levels in men or other appearance outcomes in healthy people.

Registered clinical trials of DIM concern other conditions. These include a phase 1 study in BRCA1 mutation carriers [3], a phase 1 study in men with prostate cancer that had not responded to hormone therapy [4], a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers [5], studies in breast cancer [6][7], and early studies in lupus and proliferative thyroid disease, two of which were terminated [8][9]. The registrations list design and enrolment, and the results are not summarised here.

Memorial Sloan Kettering summarises the small human studies as suggesting possible benefit in castration-resistant prostate cancer and mixed results for reversing abnormal cervical cell changes, with more research needed on safety and effectiveness [11]. It states there is no scientific evidence for the detoxification claim [11].

A US-listed homeopathic menopause product names DIM among many ingredients; its label states that its claims are based on homeopathic principles and have not been reviewed by the FDA [2]. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities, DIM is typically discussed in the context of estrogen management; no community sources were available to quote directly for this article.

lore.intro: DIM is discussed on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation as part of estrogen-management routines, though threads that name it are mostly general-chat threads and not dedicated discussions.

claims.claim: DIM shifts estrogen metabolism toward a leaner, less puffy, more androgen-dominant look
claims.believers: Marketers and supplement users in bodybuilding circles say DIM steers estrogen toward metabolites they regard as more favourable, which they associate with less water retention and a leaner appearance.
claims.experts: Memorial Sloan Kettering reports changes in urinary estrogen metabolite profiles in some women [11]. A 60-woman randomized trial found greater body-fat loss than placebo at 30 days but no significant change in the metabolite ratio [12]. No published trial has tested appearance outcomes in men.

claims.believers: Supplement marketers describe DIM as promoting the 2-hydroxy pathway over the 16-hydroxy pathway.
claims.experts: Retrospective laboratory studies report that the 2-OH to 16-OH ratio was higher in DIM users and rose after starting DIM [13], while the randomized trial did not find a significant increase at day 30 [12]. Whether the ratio predicts cancer risk is unsettled; cohort studies found no significant link [15].

claims.claim: DIM is a natural way to lower estrogen in men
claims.believers: Hormone-optimisation communities discuss DIM as an estrogen-management supplement, often alongside other products.
claims.experts: The published human studies of urinary estrogen profiles were in women [12][13][14]. No published trial has examined DIM in healthy men for hormone or appearance outcomes.

claims.claim: DIM detoxifies the body of estrogens and toxins
claims.believers: Some product marketing describes DIM as a detoxification aid.
claims.experts: Memorial Sloan Kettering states there is no scientific evidence for the detoxification claim [11].

claims.claim: DIM can interfere with medicines and hormone tests
claims.believers: Not a central claim among users.
claims.experts: Memorial Sloan Kettering reports a lowering of an active tamoxifen metabolite in one study, possible interactions via CYP450 enzymes, and that DIM may alter urinary estrogen test results [11]; a 2025 study of patch users recommends clinicians ask about DIM [14].
